abstract: Learned associations between cues and reward drive motivated behavior, yet how specific cell types support this process remains unclear. Using two-photon calcium imaging, we tracked dorsal medial prefrontal cortical astrocytes throughout the acquisition and reversal of Pavlovian sucrose conditioning. As learning progressed, astrocytes exhibited time-locked, spatially coordinated activity that differentiated correct behavior from mistakes, evolving from broad outcome encoding to selective representation of responses associated with reward-conditioned stimuli. Omission testing revealed that prefrontal astrocytes preferentially encoded the cue-reward association, rather than cue or reward alone. When reward contingencies were reversed, astrocytic activity rapidly adapted to track the new cue-reward association and encoded updated and outdated motivated behavioral actions. Finally, disrupting astrocytic coupling through hemichannel inhibition enhanced behavioral responding to the reward-paired cue across acquisition but impaired behavioral flexibility when reward contingencies were updated or unpredictable. Results reveal prefrontal astrocytes are functionally plastic elements that regulate reward seeking across associative learning.
